Machining/Milling

Climb and Conventional Milling

Which way the work is fed past a turning cutter decides whether each chip starts thick or thin, which way the cut pulls on the work, and why backlash in a feed screw matters.

Feed direction decides whether each chip starts thick or thin

Feed direction decides whether each chip starts thick or thin

A milling cutter takes metal off in small slices, one slice per tooth. Whether each slice starts thick and ends thin, or starts thin and ends thick, comes down to one thing: which way the work is fed past the turning cutter.

Climb milling
Also called down milling. Where a tooth is cutting, it moves the same way the work is fed. Each chip starts thick and ends thin.
Conventional milling
Also called up milling. Where a tooth is cutting, it moves against the feed. Each chip starts thin and ends thick.
Feed per tooth
How far the work moves while the cutter turns from one tooth to the next. It sets how thick a chip can get.
Width of cut
How far the cutter reaches into the side of the work, measured across the cutter. Machinists also call it the radial depth of cut.

How to read the drawings on this page. Each drawing is a slice straight across the fluted part of an end mill, seen looking down its axis from the spindle; the small side view in the corner marks where the slice is taken, the way a section view does on a drawing. This sketch places the cutter’s axis horizontally, with the table below it; screen-down is toward that table. It is not a top view of a vertical spindle. From the spindle end a standard right-hand cutter turns clockwise. The cutter stays where it is and the work is fed past it, the way a mill table carries the work. Every Work feed arrow is the work’s motion. On a machine that moves the cutter instead, nothing changes: the cutter simply travels the opposite way to that arrow.

The cutter is the same in both modes and spins the same way. What switches climb to conventional is the direction of feed relative to the side of the cutter that is doing the cutting. The down/up force arrows belong to this horizontal arrangement. A top view of a vertical end mill would show forces across the table, not axial force into or away from it.

Watch one tooth take its chip

Watch one tooth take its chip

The dashed gold outline is the slice of metal the cutting tooth has taken so far, drawn where it was. The solid gold shape is that metal as a chip, curling off the cutting edge into the flute. The curled chip is scaled to fit the flute at this exaggerated feed; its drawn size is not a thickness measurement. Play it, or drag the tooth through the cut, and use the dashed slice to compare thickness.

Each chip forms on the edge, rides out in the flute and is thrown clear

Each chip forms on the edge, rides out in the flute and is thrown clear

A chip does not stay where the slice was. The cutting edge shears it off the work, it slides along the face in front of the edge and curls into the flute, and the flute carries it round until it is thrown clear. Where that happens depends on the direction of feed.

Swipe the four moments sideways on a narrow screen, or focus the drawing and use the arrow keys to scroll.

Reading the cutter

  • Cutting edge: the tip of each tooth, the only part that touches the finished surface. The tooth that is cutting is outlined in blue.
  • Rake face: the face just in front of the edge. The chip slides along it as it forms.
  • Flute: the curved valley in front of each tooth. The chip curls in it and is carried out of the cut in it, so a flute packed with chips cannot take the next one.
  • Core: the solid centre, hatched because the drawing cuts through it. In this illustrated family, more flutes leave a thicker core and less room for chips. Actual proportions depend on the tool design.

The chip is drawn shorter and thinner than the slice so it fits the flute at a feed drawn many times too large. A continuous metal chip usually becomes shorter and thicker through deformation; IIT Kharagpur’s chip-formation lesson explains the change. The path it takes is illustrative; coolant, tool geometry and the material affect actual chip motion. The cutter’s flutes and chip space follow Harvey Performance’s end mill anatomy.

Six things to try in the demo

Six things to try in the demo

  • Choose Compare both and step until each tooth has only just entered the work. Which chip is already thick, and which is barely there?
  • Drag Tooth position in the cut from 0% to 100%, once in each mode. Watch the uncut-thickness readout: in climb it runs down from the peak, in conventional it runs up to it.
  • Set the width of cut to 50%. The tooth now cuts through a quarter of a turn and the chip reaches the full feed per tooth. Drop it to 10%: the peak falls to 60% of the feed. At the same feed, a narrower cut makes a thinner chip.
  • Raise the feed per tooth and watch the dashed uncut slice grow thicker. Its thick-to-thin trend stays the same. The curled chip is scaled to fit the flute and may stop growing on screen; compare thickness using the dashed slice.
  • Follow one chip from start to finish. Pause just before a tooth leaves the work, then step forward. In which mode is the thick end of the chip at the curled tip, and in which is it still on the edge? Where does each chip go once it is free?
  • Watch the red-orange arrow, the pull of the cut on the work. In climb it pulls the work the way it is already going and presses it down. In conventional it pushes back against the feed and lifts. Keep that in mind for the card on backlash.
Starting thin means rubbing; starting thick means a bite

Starting thin means rubbing; starting thick means a bite

A real cutting edge has a rounded tip. When the uncut layer is extremely thin, the edge can push and rub the metal before a chip forms. The peripheral cuts shown here make that difference visible.

  • Conventional milling starts every chip at zero, so every tooth rubs before it bites. Rubbing makes heat and wears the edge. Look at where the tooth enters, too: on the finished surface, the one you are keeping.
  • Climb milling starts the chips shown here at their thickest, so the tooth bites at once, with a knock each time a tooth enters.

That is the main reason climb milling is often the preferred direction when the machine can hold the work steady against it. Whether it can is the next card.

Which way the cut pulls on the work

  • Climb: the teeth drag the work along the way it is already being fed, and tend to push it down onto the table in the peripheral arrangement shown.
  • Conventional: the teeth push back against the feed and tend to lift the work in this arrangement, so whatever holds the work has to resist that lift.
Backlash: why climb milling depends on the machine

Backlash: why climb milling depends on the machine

A feed screw moves the table by turning inside a nut. Unless the drive is built to take it out, there is some clearance between the screw’s thread and the nut. That clearance is called backlash, and it lets the table shift a little while the screw stands still.

  • Conventional: the cut pushes the table back, against the feed. That holds the nut against the flank of the thread the screw is driving with, so the gap stays on the far side and the table moves only as fast as the screw turns.
  • Climb: the cut pulls the table forward, the way it is already moving. If there is clearance, the table can slide across it ahead of the screw, and the cutter takes a bigger bite than the feed was set for, all at once. That sudden, oversized bite is hard on the cutter and on whatever is holding the work.

This is a question to ask about a machine, not a rule. How much clearance a feed drive has, and whether it is built to take it out, differs from machine to machine. This page does not tell you which direction to use on any machine you will meet. Ask the person responsible for that machine.

Supporting detail: Addendum 1 — Why some machines climb mill without trouble.

A slot is both at once

A slot is both at once

When the cutter is buried across its whole width, cutting a slot, each tooth enters at one wall and leaves at the other. Its chip starts thin, is thickest halfway across, and ends thin. The first half of the sweep moves against the feed, like conventional milling, and the second half moves with it, like climb milling, whichever way the work is fed. That is why the demo stops at half the cutter’s diameter: past that point the two can no longer be pulled apart.

Machining/Milling

Feeds and Speeds

How a cutting speed and a cutter diameter set the spindle speed, how the spindle speed, flute count and chip load set the table feed, how width, depth and feed set the volume of metal removed, and how that volume and the material set the cutting power.

Two numbers come from cutting data; two go into the machine

Two numbers come from cutting data; two go into the machine

A milling setup is described by four numbers. Two describe what each cutting edge goes through, and they come from cutting data for the tool and the material. The other two are what you actually set on the machine, and you work them out from the first two.

Cutting speed
How fast the cutting edge moves through the material: the speed at the outside of the cutter. Written in surface feet per minute (SFM) or metres per minute (m/min). Also called surface speed. Comes from cutting data.
Feed per tooth
How far the work moves while the cutter turns from one tooth to the next, in inches or millimetres per tooth. Also called chip load, because it sets the size of the bite each tooth takes. Comes from cutting data.
Spindle speed
How many turns the cutter makes each minute, in revolutions per minute (rev/min, usually said RPM). Set on the machine.
Table feed
How fast the work moves past the cutter, in inches or millimetres per minute. Also called the feed rate. On a machine that moves the cutter instead, it is how fast the cutter travels. Set on the machine.

"Speeds" are the cutter turning; "feeds" are the work moving. That is all the phrase feeds and speeds means. The two are set separately on the machine, and the rest of this page is about how they depend on each other, how much metal they remove, and the power that takes.

Spindle speed: the turns it takes to reach the cutting speed

Spindle speed: the turns it takes to reach the cutting speed

Cutting speed is a distance per minute, measured at the edge of the cutter. In one turn, a point on that edge travels once around the cutter: its circumference, π × D. So the spindle speed is the cutting speed divided by the distance one turn covers, once the two are in the same units.

Spindle speed (rev/min) = 12 × cutting speed (SFM) ÷ (π × cutter diameter in inches)

The 12 is there because cutting speed is in feet and the diameter is in inches: 12 inches to the foot. In metric units the same idea needs a 1000, millimetres to the metre:

Spindle speed (rev/min) = 1000 × cutting speed (m/min) ÷ (π × cutter diameter in mm)

Worked example, with illustrative numbers. A 0.5 in cutter, with cutting data that calls for 300 SFM: 12 × 300 ÷ (π × 0.5) = 2,292 rev/min. The 300 SFM is there to make the arithmetic concrete. It is not a recommendation for any tool or any material. The feed value below is illustrative too; use the later material guide for the carbide starting bands.

Look at where the diameter sits: underneath. Halve the diameter and the spindle speed doubles. A small cutter has to turn faster to give its edge the same cutting speed, which is why small cutters so often ask for more speed than a machine has. That case has its own card below.

Table feed: each tooth takes one chip load as it passes

Table feed: each tooth takes one chip load as it passes

Each time a tooth passes, the work should have moved one feed per tooth. The number of teeth passing each minute is the spindle speed times the number of flutes, so:

Table feed = spindle speed × flutes × feed per tooth

Worked example, continued. A 4-flute cutter at 2,292 rev/min, with a feed per tooth of 0.002 in: 2,292 × 4 × 0.002 = 18.3 in/min. The units work out on their own: turns per minute, times teeth per turn, times inches per tooth, leaves inches per minute.

Turned around, the same relation tells you what chip load a feed gives. That is the way to check a feed someone else has set:

Feed per tooth = table feed ÷ (spindle speed × flutes)

Flutes here means the teeth that actually take a chip in each turn. For an ordinary end mill that is simply the number of flutes.

Removal rate: width × depth × table feed

Removal rate: width × depth × table feed

Two more numbers describe the cut itself. The width of cut is how far the cutter reaches sideways into the work, across the direction of feed. The depth of cut is how far down its side the cutter is buried, along its axis. A side cut can be no wider than the cutter; a wider path takes more than one pass.

While the table feeds, the cutter sweeps through the work and leaves a channel behind it. In a stretch of time the cutter travels table feed × time, and the solid metal it takes out in that stretch is a slab as wide as the cut, as deep as the cut, and as long as that travel. Per minute, that is the material removal rate:

Removal rate (in³/min) = width of cut (in) × depth of cut (in) × table feed (in/min)

The front of the cut is curved, because it is the cutter’s own shape. The slab’s two ends are the same curve, one travel apart, so whatever the curve, the slab holds exactly width × depth × travel.

Worked example, continued. The same cutter, 0.1 in wide (20% of its diameter) and 0.5 in deep, at 18.3 in/min: 0.1 × 0.5 × 18.3 ≈ 0.917 in³/min, or 15.0 cm³/min. In 5 seconds the cutter travels 1.53 in and removes 0.0764 in³.

That is the volume of solid metal. Once it is chips, the same metal lies loose and takes up far more space, so the removal rate is not the size of the chip pile.

Cutting power: removal rate times the energy each cubic inch takes

Cutting power: removal rate times the energy each cubic inch takes

Cutting a cubic inch of a given material takes roughly a given amount of energy. That is its specific cutting energy, and it is why the same cut needs more power in steel than in aluminum. Written as power per unit of removal rate, it turns a removal rate straight into power:

Cutting power (hp) = removal rate (in³/min) × unit power (hp per in³/min)

Cutting power (W) = removal rate (mm³/min) × specific energy (J/mm³) ÷ 60

The 60 turns minutes into seconds, because a watt is a joule per second. One mechanical horsepower is 745.7 W.

Worked example, continued. For 6061-T6 aluminum the guide in the calculator gives a band of 0.16 to 0.30 hp per in³/min. At 0.917 in³/min that is about 0.15 to 0.28 hp, or 110 to 210 W. The same cut in 304 stainless steel, whose band is 0.65 to 1.3 hp per in³/min, needs about 0.60 to 1.2 hp.

The answer is usually a band. Some table rows give one factor; that still produces an estimate, not a measured certainty. Published bands cover a family of materials over a range of hardness, and the energy a real cut takes also depends on chip thickness and cutting-edge geometry. Treat the band as the size of the job, not a prediction to the watt.

Three different powers get called “the power”, and they are not the same:

  • Cutting power is what the cutting edge spends. That is the estimate above.
  • Motor shaft power is more, because the belts, gears and bearings between the motor and the cutter lose some on the way. If the drivetrain passes on 80% of what the motor delivers, the motor must deliver the cutting power ÷ 0.8.
  • Electrical power drawn from the supply is more again, because the motor and its drive lose some too.

None of these tells you whether a machine can take the cut. A spindle motor’s rating is not necessarily available at every speed, and power is only one limit: the tool, the holding and the machine’s stiffness are others. Use the estimate to compare cuts and to see why a cut is heavy, not to approve one.

Calculator: from material guidance to removal and power

Calculator: from material guidance to removal and power

Choose a material to see generic carbide starting ranges for it, then enter the cutter, the cutting data and the cut. Nothing is filled in for you. Each result appears as soon as the fields it needs are filled, and says what it is still waiting for until then. Use the middle of these ranges fills in only the cutting speed and feed per tooth.

How to read the drawings. You are looking at a block of work from the front, a little above and to the right. The cutter feeds to the right along the front top edge. Gold is the solid metal removed in the time shown, drawn where it was before the cutter took it. The dashed blue curve is where the front of the cut stood when that time began; the outlined cylinder is the cutter now. The three labeled axes use the same length scale, and the drawings in one comparison share that scale, so a slab twice as long is twice the volume. The block around the cut is there only to hold it; its size means nothing. The cut is already underway when the interval starts; only the gold volume counts toward that interval.

The comparison below the drawings prices the setup’s removal rate in every material. The cut is the same in every row; only the energy per cubic inch changes.

Things to try in the calculator

Things to try in the calculator

  • Before typing anything, read the results. Each one names the fields it is waiting for.
  • With 6061-T6 aluminum chosen, enter a 0.5 in diameter and 4 flutes, then press Use the middle of these ranges. Cutting speed and feed per tooth fill in at 400 SFM and 0.00415 in/tooth. Nothing else changes.
  • Enter a width of 0.1 in and a depth of 0.5 in. Check the removal rate against width × depth × table feed in the arithmetic.
  • Change the material to 304 stainless steel. The drawings, the table feed and the removal rate stay exactly as they were; only the power estimate moves. The guide now marks your cutting speed as above its range for stainless, but the calculator leaves your entries alone.
  • Hold the table feed and drag the spindle speed to 200%. The slab does not change and nor does the removal rate: the same metal comes off, in chips half as thick.
  • Now hold the chip load and do the same. The table feed doubles, the slab grows twice as long in the same time, and the removal rate and power estimate double.
  • Switch to metric and back. The cut and every result stay the same, written in other units, and any field you left empty stays empty.
  • Try a width larger than the diameter. The calculator refuses it: that is more than one pass.
  • Enter a 0.125 in cutter with a 4,000 rev/min machine top speed. Compare the speed the cutting speed asks for with the speed the machine can reach, and where the cutting speed actually reached sits against the guide.
When the machine cannot turn as fast as the formula asks

When the machine cannot turn as fast as the formula asks

Because small cutters ask for high spindle speeds, the formula can easily give more than a machine’s top speed. A 0.125 in cutter at 300 SFM asks for 9,167 rev/min. On a machine that stops at 4,000, it runs at 4,000.

  • Work the feed from the speed the spindle really turns. At 4,000 rev/min, with 2 flutes and 0.0008 in per tooth, that is 4,000 × 2 × 0.0008 = 6.4 in/min. Each tooth then takes the chip load you meant it to.
  • The cutting speed is what you give up. At 4,000 rev/min the edge of a 0.125 in cutter moves at π × 0.125 × 4,000 ÷ 12 = 131 SFM, not the 300 the data asked for.

Working the feed from the speed that was asked for, rather than the one the spindle is turning, gets the chip load wrong by the same ratio. A feed worked from 9,167 rev/min would give each tooth 9,167 ÷ 4,000 = 2.3 times the chip load intended.

The same applies to a machine that offers only certain speeds, through belts or gears: set the nearest speed it has, and work the feed from that one. The calculator’s machine top speed box does this for a top speed.

Generic ranges are a starting point, not your tool’s data

Generic ranges are a starting point, not your tool’s data

What determines the surface speed?

Start with the material and its hardness, then the cutting tool. Carbide is a tool material, not one universal cutting edge: its grade, coating and geometry matter, as do coolant and how steadily the setup can cut. A harder material generally calls for a lower starting speed. Once that surface speed is chosen, the diameter determines the RPM; a smaller cutter must turn faster to reach the same surface speed.

What determines the feed per tooth?

Choose a bite the cutting edge can carry and the flute can clear. That is why the guide changes with cutter diameter: small cutters generally take smaller bites. Width and depth of cut, a full-width slot, a long tool and a flexible setup change the loading and chip clearance. The number of flutes then tells you how many of those bites happen per turn; it does not by itself choose the size of each bite. Use the diameter-based range as a starting point, with its stated engagement, and refine it from the actual tool’s cutting data.

The arithmetic on this page is exact. Its inputs are the part that takes judgement. The ranges in the calculator are generic starting bands for solid-carbide end mills, by material family, from published toolmaker tables. The cutting data for your tool comes first: normally the toolmaker’s for that tool, that material and that kind of cut, or the person responsible for the machine.

Cutting data accounts for things these formulas cannot see: the exact grade and hardness of the material, the tool’s coating and geometry, how far it reaches out of the holder, coolant, and how the setup is held. The guide’s feed-per-tooth ranges assume a side cut about 20% of the cutter’s diameter wide; a full-width slot or a long reach needs the tool’s own data. A calculator turns data into machine settings. It cannot tell you whether the data suit your cut.

Supporting detail: Addendum 2 — Feed per tooth is not always the thickness of the chip.

Machining/Milling

G-code and Toolpaths

How a CNC mill reads a program line by line: rapid and feed moves, absolute and incremental coordinates, units, arcs and a drilling cycle. Build a program from blocks and watch it cut a simulated block.

A CNC program is a list of lines, and each line tells the machine one thing to do

A CNC program is a list of lines, and each line tells the machine one thing to do

A CNC mill moves its tool by reading a program from the top down, one line at a time. The language most mills read is called G-code. Each line holds a few words, and together they say where the tool goes next, how fast, and what the spindle and tool are doing.

Word
A letter and a number, such as X20, G1 or F300. The letter says what the number means: X, Y and Z are positions, F is the feed rate, S the spindle speed, T a tool number. G and M words are codes that choose what kind of move or machine action the line is.
Block
One line of the program. Machinists often call a line a block; in the simulator below, each block you snap into place is one line of G-code, with the same number.
Work zero
The point the program’s numbers count from. Here, as in Milling Operations, X 0, Y 0 is the front left corner of the block and Z 0 is its finished top face. The uncut stock starts at Z +1. Positions refer to the tip of the tool, on its centre line: Z −3 is 3 mm below work zero and 4 mm below that raw top. A pointed drill reaches its programmed Z at its tip; the full-diameter hole is shallower.
Modal
Most codes stay in force until another code from their group replaces them. After a G1, a line with only X80 is still a G1 move; a feed rate set once with F is used by every feed move after it. A word a line leaves out keeps the value it had.

Read the program above from the top. Line 2 sets millimetres, absolute positions and the XY plane. Line 3 puts tool 1, a Ø10 end mill, in the spindle, and line 4 starts the spindle at 2500 rpm. Lines 5 and 6 move the tool through the air to just above the start of the slot. Line 7 feeds it to Z −3, cutting 4 mm below the raw top at Z +1. Line 8 feeds it along the closed-ended slot, and line 9 lifts it clear. Line 10 stops the spindle and line 11 ends the program.

Rapid moves put the tool in place through the air; feed moves cut

Rapid moves put the tool in place through the air; feed moves cut

  • G0 is a rapid move. The machine moves as fast as it can. It is for getting the tool to where a cut starts, through the air, never for cutting.
  • G1 is a feed move. The tool moves in a straight line at the feed rate set by F, here in millimetres per minute. This is the move that cuts.
  • The spindle has to be turning first. S sets its speed in revolutions per minute, M3 starts it turning clockwise seen from above, and M5 stops it. T1 M6 changes to tool 1.
  • A move goes in one straight line. G1 X80 Y40 Z-2 moves all three axes together and they all arrive at once. An axis left out of the line stays where it is: G1 X80 moves along X only.

A rapid into metal is a crash: the tool arrives at full traverse speed with nothing to say it should be cutting. The simulator stops a rapid at the point where it would touch the block and says so. It does the same if a feed move reaches the metal with the spindle stopped.

This simulator moves a rapid in one straight line, the way the LinuxCNC G-code reference describes G0. Controls differ in how they move during a rapid, so check how the one you use moves before you count on the path a rapid takes.

G90 and G91, G20 and G21: two modes that change what every number means

G90 and G91, G20 and G21: two modes that change what every number means

G90, absolute
A number is a position, measured from work zero. With the tool at X 10, G1 X30 moves it to X 30.
G91, incremental
A number is a distance from where the tool is now. With the tool at X 10, the same G1 X30 moves it 30 mm, to X 40.
G21, millimetres
X30 means 30 mm and F300 means 300 mm per minute.
G20, inches
The same X30 means 30 inches, which is 762 mm, and the feed rate is in inches per minute. A millimetre program read in inches asks for moves 25.4 times as long.

Because these modes change the meaning of every line after them, a program sets both near its start, before the first move. The simulator insists on it: a move before G20 or G21 and G90 or G91 have been set stops the program, and so does a change of units after the machine has started moving.

G2 turns clockwise and G3 counterclockwise, seen from above

G2 turns clockwise and G3 counterclockwise, seen from above

An arc move cuts along part of a circle in the XY plane (G17) at the feed rate. Its direction is the way it turns as seen looking down on the work from above: G2 clockwise, G3 counterclockwise. The line gives the arc’s end point with X and Y, and its centre in one of two ways.

  • I and J say where the centre is, measured in X and Y from the point where the arc starts. That is the usual mode, G91.1, and it holds even while G90 makes every X and Y a position. G90.1 makes I and J a position too.
  • R gives the radius instead, and the control works out the centre. A positive R is the arc of less than half a turn, a negative R the longer way round. An R arc cannot be a full circle, because a circle through one point has no single centre; a full circle uses I and J with its end point the same as its start.

Worked example. The tool is at X 72, Y 15, moving right along the bottom of an outline. G3 X80 Y23 I0 J8 puts the centre 0 in X and 8 in Y from the start, at X 72, Y 23. Turning counterclockwise about it, the tool rounds a corner of radius 8 and ends heading up the right-hand side at X 80, Y 23. The end point has to lie on the circle: change J8 to J6 and the end is 2 mm from where the circle goes, so the simulator stops at that line instead of guessing.

A drilling cycle packs a whole hole into one line

A drilling cycle packs a whole hole into one line

G81 X15 Y15 Z-8 R2 F120 drills a hole at X 15, Y 15. The tool moves there at rapid, comes down at rapid to R, the height just above the work where feeding begins, feeds down to Z, the bottom of the hole, and rises back up at rapid.

  • How high it rises. In this simulator G99 rises to R between holes, and G98 rises to the height the tool was at when the cycles began, or to R if that is higher. The simulator needs one of the two before the first G81.
  • The cycle is modal. After a G81, a line with only X or Y drills another hole with the same depth, R and feed. G80 ends the cycle; after it, a line with only X or Y is an error until a G0 or G1 says how to move.
The program is the path of the tool’s centre, not the edge of the part

The program is the path of the tool’s centre, not the edge of the part

Every X and Y in a program says where the centre of the tool goes. The metal is cut by its edge, one radius further out. A Ø10 end mill fed along Y 30 cuts a slot from Y 25 to Y 35. To leave a wall at X 80 with the metal beyond it cut away, the centre runs along X 85. Milling Operations works through the same rule for a shoulder and a pocket.

Controls can do that offset for you with cutter radius compensation, G41 and G42. The simulator does not model it, so every program here is written as the path of the centre, and a line with G41 or G42 stops with a message.

Simulator: build a program from blocks and watch it run

Simulator: build a program from blocks and watch it run

Pick a program, change it, and run it on a simulated block of metal in a vise. Every block is one line of G-code; the same interpreter reads it whether you build it from blocks or type it, and the machine runs exactly what it reads.

How to drive it. Press a block in the program to open it and change its numbers; leave a number empty to leave that word out of the line. Add a block from the row above the program, either by pressing it, which puts it after the open block, or by dragging it into place. Drag a block by its handle to move it; with the keyboard, focus the handle and press Alt with ↑ or ↓. Play runs the program, Step runs one block and stops, Back goes back one block and Restart starts again with fresh stock. The block that is running is outlined in gold, and its move is drawn in gold on the views; press a move in the top view to open the block that makes it. Any change to the program puts the simulation back to its start, so it always shows the program as it now is.

Things to try in the G-code simulator

Things to try in the G-code simulator

  • Step through the slot program one block at a time. Watch the machine state change at blocks 2, 3 and 4 before anything moves.
  • Make the slot deeper and shorter, then run it again. Which numbers did you change?
  • Drag the Spindle on block below the first feed move, and read why the machine stops.
  • Open block 7 of the slot program and switch it from G1 to G0. What does a rapid do when it meets the metal?
  • Change the slot program to G91. Before you press Play, work out where its first move will go.
  • In the arcs program, swap one G3 for a G2, and see which way that corner turns now.
  • In the holes program, try G99 instead of G98, then add a fifth hole.
  • In the G-code text, type a line the simulator does not read, such as G41 or M7, and read what it says.
What the simulator reads, and what it leaves out

What the simulator reads, and what it leaves out

The simulator reads a small part of G-code, modelled on the way the LinuxCNC control reads it. Any other code, or a line that is not G-code at all, stops the program at that line with a message saying what is wrong. Nothing is skipped.

Motion
G0 rapid, G1 feed, G2 and G3 arcs in the XY plane, G81 drilling cycle and G80 to end it.
Modes
G17 XY plane, G20 inches, G21 millimetres, G90 absolute, G91 incremental, G90.1 and G91.1 for I and J, G94 feed per minute, G98 and G99 for the drilling cycle. G40, G49 and G54 are read as the settings the simulator always has: no cutter compensation, no tool length offset, and its one work offset.
Machine
M3 spindle on, M5 off, M6 tool change, M8 and M9 coolant on and off (shown, with no effect on the cut), M2 or M30 program end: stops spindle and coolant, restores G90 and G1, and leaves the tool at its last position.
Words
X Y Z positions, I J arc centre, R arc radius or drilling R plane, F feed rate, S spindle speed, T tool, N line number, and comments in brackets or after a semicolon.
Tools
T1 Ø10 end mill, T2 Ø6 end mill, T3 Ø6 drill, T4 Ø12 spot and chamfer tool, T5 Ø50 face mill: the tools of Milling Operations, with the same rules about what each can cut.
  • Some rules are the simulator’s own. It needs units and distance mode set before the first move, a speed before M3, G98 or G99 before a drilling cycle, and, for a tool change, the spindle stopped and the tool at Z +20 or higher. A real control may be less strict, or strict about different things.
  • Only straight down and straight across, through metal. The block is modelled as a height above each point, so the tool can cut moving along Z alone, or in X and Y at one height. A move in X or Y and Z at once is followed exactly through the air, but stops if it would reach the metal: ramping and helical moves are not modelled.
  • Arcs are cut as short straight chords, each within 0.01 mm of the true arc. They are drawn as true arcs.
  • Simple timing. Feed moves run at their F and rapids at 5000 mm per minute, with no acceleration, no blending of one move into the next, and no time for tool changes.
  • Not a check of a real program. The speeds and feeds in the examples are round teaching numbers, not cutting recommendations; Feeds and Speeds is about choosing them. A program that runs here has met only this simulator’s rules. Controls differ in the codes they accept, in their starting modes and in how they change tools, so a program for a real machine is checked against the manual for its control.

Supporting detail: Addendum 3 — How the simulator reads and runs a program.

Machining/Milling

Milling Operations

Make a part on a simulated vertical mill: choose each tool, move it through the metal, and check what is left against the drawing. Facing, shoulders, pockets, slots, drilled, tapped and bored holes, countersinks and chamfers.

A vertical mill shapes a block with a turning tool moved in X, Y and Z

A vertical mill shapes a block with a turning tool moved in X, Y and Z

On a vertical mill the cutting tool turns in a spindle above the work. The work is clamped on the table, the table moves it front to back and side to side, and the tool comes down into it. Every shape the mill makes is the space the turning tool swept through.

X and Y
The two directions across the table. In this lesson X runs left to right as you face the machine and Y runs away from you, toward the back.
Z
Up and down, along the tool. Z+ is up, away from the work, so negative Z is below the finished top face. The raw top is at Z +1, so facing can remove metal at zero or positive Z while taking off that allowance.
Readout
The display that shows where the tool is, in X, Y and Z. A readout on a manual mill is often called a DRO, for digital readout. Here it shows the position of the tool’s tip.
Work zero
The point the readout counts from. In this lesson X 0, Y 0 is the front left corner of the block and Z 0 is the finished top face. Every dimension on the drawings is measured from those same edges and that same face.

On a real knee mill the table carries the work under a spindle that stays put in X and Y. In the simulator you move the tool instead. The readout tells the same story either way: where the tool’s tip is, measured from work zero.

Each kind of tool cuts a shape of its own, and some cannot cut sideways

Each kind of tool cuts a shape of its own, and some cannot cut sideways

Face mill
A wide body with cutting inserts round its rim. It is fed across the work to leave a broad flat face. The one in the simulator takes at most 4 mm in one pass. The inserts sit at the rim, not across the middle, so it is brought down beside the work and then fed in, never pushed straight down into the metal.
End mill
Cuts on its sides and its end. The end mills here are centre-cutting: their end teeth reach the middle, so they can be fed straight down into the metal and then moved across to cut pockets, slots, steps and walls. An inside corner they leave is rounded to the cutter’s own radius.
Spot and chamfer tool
A pointed tool with a 90° point. Fed down, it cuts a cone: the start of a hole, or a countersink round the mouth of one. Run along an edge, it bevels the edge, which is a chamfer.
Drill
Cuts only at its point, as it feeds down along its own axis. It leaves a round hole its own size, with a cone at the bottom from its point. It must never be pushed sideways in the metal.
Tap
Cuts a screw thread into the wall of a hole that is already there. It only goes straight in and straight back out.
Boring head
An adjustable single cutting point on an offset bar. Set to a diameter and fed down a hole, it opens the hole to that size. Its bar has no cutting edge at the centre, so it needs a hole to start in.

This is a teaching rack, not a list of what to buy or use. The sizes are illustrative. A real cutter’s length, number of teeth and depth of cut come from its own data and from the person responsible for the machine.

The tool’s centre runs one radius away from the wall it cuts

The tool’s centre runs one radius away from the wall it cuts

The readout shows where the centre of the tool is. The metal is cut by its edge. To leave a wall at a given place, put the centre one radius away from it, on the side being cut away.

Worked example. A shoulder’s wall belongs at X 75, with the metal to the right of it cut away. A Ø12 end mill has a 6 mm radius, so its centre runs along X 75 + 6 = X 81. Run it along X 75 instead and the wall ends up at X 69, 6 mm too far into the part. That metal cannot be put back.

  • Inside corners take the cutter’s radius. A round tool cannot reach into a sharp inside corner, so a pocket’s corners come out rounded to the radius of the cutter that made them. A drawing that allows R4 at most calls for a cutter no bigger than Ø8.
  • Outside corners stay sharp. Going round the outside of a corner, the tool swings about it and never cuts into it.
  • A slot is the width of the cutter that made it in one pass. A cutter moved in a straight line leaves a groove exactly its own width, with round ends of its own radius.

When a cutter cuts with its side, the metal is on one side of it or the other. With the cutter turning clockwise seen from above, metal on the cutter’s right as it moves is climb milling, and metal on its left is conventional milling. The simulator says which each side cut was. Climb and Conventional Milling explains the difference.

Holes: drilled to size, threaded by a tap, opened up by a boring head

Holes: drilled to size, threaded by a tap, opened up by a boring head

A drill leaves a hole of its own diameter. A hole’s depth on a drawing is measured to where the hole stops being full size, not to the tip of the cone the drill point leaves below that.

A tapped hole starts as a smaller drilled hole

A tap cuts its thread into the wall of a hole, so the hole has to be drilled smaller than the thread first, to the tap drill size. For the common metric coarse threads that size is close to the thread’s outside diameter minus its pitch, the distance from one thread to the next:

Tap drill ≈ thread diameter − pitch. M6×1: 6 − 1 = Ø5.0. M8×1.25: 8 − 1.25 = Ø6.75, drilled Ø6.8.

Drilled too small, the tap has to cut too much metal and can break. Drilled too big, the thread is shallow. The simulator checks the hole against a simplified minor-diameter band and refuses a severely undersize pilot. This does not establish functional thread fit: pitch diameter, thread form and a real thread gauge are separate checks.

Drill deeper than the thread you need

The first few threads of a tap are ground away to a taper so that it can start in the hole. Those threads cut only part of a thread, so full thread stops short of the tap’s tip. In a hole with a bottom, the tap has to go deeper than the full thread you need, and the drilled hole deeper again, past the drill’s point. This simulated tap has a 4-pitch cutting chamfer; real taps vary. The job calls for full thread reaching Z −10 from the finished face. Its countersink removes the first part of the thread, so that is not 10 mm of surviving full-thread length.

Sizes no drill gives

Drills come in fixed sizes. A boring head is set to the size you need and fed down a hole already big enough for its bar, which makes it the tool for a hole of an exact, larger size.

Simulator: make the part on the drawing, then inspect it

Simulator: make the part on the drawing, then inspect it

Pick a job, choose a tool and move it through the block. The finished part is drawn over the block you are cutting: gold is metal still to remove, stronger where there is more of it, and striped red-orange is metal cut past the drawing. The inspection measures the part that is left after every move. Nothing checks which tools you used or in what order: any way of making the right part passes.

How to drive it. Choose a kind of tool, then its size. Drag the tool’s circle in the top view to move it in X and Y, or drag the tool in the section to move it up and down. The switch at the top of the views changes between Top and front, the top view with its section, and Isometric, the part in 3D, which turns to show every side; the finished part is marked in both. To go to an exact place, type X, Y and Z under Move to and press Move; the tool goes up before it goes across, and across before it goes down. The handwheel buttons and the arrow keys move one step at a time. A move that would break a tool or hit the vise stops where it would happen, and says why. Undo takes back the last move: the one thing a real mill cannot do.

Things to try in the simulator

Things to try in the simulator

  • In job 1, load the face mill, move it over the block and try to lower it straight onto the metal. Read why it stops.
  • Lower the face mill to Z 0.00 beside the block and drag it across. Watch the top view and the sections: the raw top is 1 mm above Z 0. Overlap a second pass until the top face check matches.
  • Cut the shoulder with the Ø12 end mill with its centre on X 75 instead of X 81. Read the inspection, then use Undo and cut it again in the right place.
  • In job 2, clear the pocket with the Ø12 end mill and read what the inspection says about its corners. Undo, and clear it with a smaller cutter.
  • Watch the gold as you cut: it is metal the drawing does not keep. Cut one pass a little too deep and see where the striped red-orange appears in the top view and the section.
  • In job 3, try to tap a hole you drilled with the Ø6.0 drill, then one you drilled with the Ø4.2. Then drill Ø5.0 only 10 mm deep and tap it as deep as it will go. How much full thread do you get?
  • In job 4, try the boring head before there is any hole. Then drill one first.
  • Make one part two different ways, for example job 4 with the face mill doing the area round the boss, and again with an end mill. Both pass.
What the simulator leaves out

What the simulator leaves out

The simulator is a model of where metal is and where tools can reach. It does not check speeds, feeds, forces or finish, and passing a job here says nothing about whether a real setup could take the same cuts. Feeds and Speeds is about those numbers.

  • Only straight down and straight across. The tool axis is always vertical and nothing is undercut, so every shape is a height above each point of the table.
  • Tools are exact and rigid. A hole is exactly the drill’s size, a cutter never bends or wears, and edges come out without burrs.
  • Threads are recorded, not drawn. The simulator keeps the size of the hole a thread was cut in and how deep its full thread runs, and checks that later cuts have not taken the metal it is in. It does not model the thread’s form or fit.
  • No chips, coolant or heat, and no limit on depth of cut except where a tool’s cutting edges run out.

Supporting detail: Addendum 4 — How the inspection decides, and what its numbers are.

Machining/Milling

Tool Stickout and Deflection

A longer tool reaches farther, but bends much more under the same sideways load. Predict a change, test it, and compare the tool with a fixed baseline.

Experiment: how much does a shorter tool help?

Experiment: how much does a shorter tool help?

Predict first: keep the same solid tool, force and material. If its unsupported length drops from 80 to 40 mm, will it bend half as much, one eighth as much, or the same amount?

The length that matters starts at the clamp

The length that matters starts at the clamp

Stickout is unsupported length. Here it is the distance from the rigid clamp face to the point where the sideways force acts. It is not the total tool length, and it is not automatically the flute length.

A force bends the tool and moves its cutting edge away from its unloaded position. The clamp end stays in place and keeps its direction; the bend grows along the unsupported length. In a real cut, force acts over the engaged cutting edges rather than at one perfect point.

Reach is a tradeoff. The tool must reach the feature and clear the work and holder. Within those constraints, reducing unnecessary stickout improves bending stiffness. A larger diameter can also help if the feature has room for it.

Length is cubed; diameter is raised to the fourth power

Length is cubed; diameter is raised to the fourth power

For the ideal solid round tool in this lab, tip bending is proportional to F × L³ ÷ (E × d⁴). Change one input at a time to see which factor is responsible.

½ length → ⅛ bendHalf × half × half. Shortening the unsupported reach is a powerful change.
2× diameter → ¹⁄₁₆ bend2 × 2 × 2 × 2 goes into the denominator. This comparison is for solid round sections.
2× force → 2× bendForce acts linearly. Double E instead, with the other inputs fixed, and bending halves.

Try a combined change: start at L = 40 mm and d = 10 mm, save that baseline, then set L = 80 mm and d = 20 mm. The length contributes 8× and the diameter contributes 1/16×, leaving half the bending at the same load and modulus. The two changes compete.

Supporting detail: Addendum 5 — The calculation and its units.

Use the trend; know what this model leaves out

Use the trend; know what this model leaves out

This is a static, linear-elastic, slender-beam model: a uniform solid round tool, a perfectly rigid clamp, a steady sideways point load at the free end and deflections small compared with the length. Elastic modulus E measures stiffness, not hardness or breaking strength.

The lab starts at E = 600 GPa, a chosen teaching value within Hyperion's published 430–690 GPa range for cemented-carbide wear grades. It is not a universal value for carbide cutters. The force is an assumed input, not calculated from a milling operation.

Flutes and necks change stiffness. The holder, spindle and workpiece can move too, and a milling force changes as teeth engage. Static bending alone does not predict chatter thresholds, surface roughness, fracture, safe loads or guaranteed finished-part error.

The lab flags L/d below 4 and bending above 1% of L as prompts to question this simplification. Those are teaching checks, not certification or safety limits.

Supporting detail: Addendum 6 — Primary references.

Connect the setup to feeds, speeds and removal rate, and explore the path and tool access in Milling Operations.

Machining/Turning

Lathe Operations

What each lathe tool does and cannot do, why most parts start with a facing cut and end with parting, and a simulator to make four parts from bar.

A lathe spins the work and moves the tool on two slides

A lathe spins the work and moves the tool on two slides

In ordinary turning the work rotates while the tool feeds along it or toward its center. This simulator models parts that are round about the spindle’s axis. The shape comes from where the tool is put against the turning work, and in what order.

Chuck
Grips the bar and turns with the spindle. The jaws hold one end; the tool works on the part of the bar that sticks out.
Carriage (Z)
Carries the tool along the bed, parallel to the axis. On this page Z minus is toward the chuck and Z plus toward the tailstock.
Cross slide (X)
Moves the tool straight toward or away from the axis. The simulator’s X readout is the diameter the tool would cut. On a real lathe, find out whether a dial or readout shows diameter or radius before you trust it.
Tailstock
At the far end of the bed, on the centerline. It holds the center drill, the drills and the countersink, which feed straight along the axis.
Z0
Where the drawing’s finished front face belongs. Every length on the drawings is measured from the front face.

How to read the simulator’s picture. It is the lathe seen from the front, with the whole work in one of two views; the switch under the picture changes view at any time without changing the work. Section cuts the work in half along its centerline, the way a section drawing shows a part: metal is hatched, a hole shows open, and a thread or knurl shows as its profile. Normal shows the outside, as you would see the part on the machine, with its thread and knurl; a hole is drawn as a dashed hidden line, and a tool working inside the part is hidden by it. Tools on the cross slide come in from above, in the plane the section is cut on, so a tool and the metal it cuts are in the same plane.

The dashed blue outline is the drawing, placed at Z0. Tinted metal is still to come off. A heavy red-orange dashed line marks work that is already smaller than the drawing allows. On each tool, the gold edge is the part that cuts and the small ring is the point the readout follows.

Before using a real lathe, read Machine Hazards and Housekeeping. The chuck key stays in your hand until it is out of the chuck.

Lathe simulator: make the part on the drawing

Lathe simulator: make the part on the drawing

Pick a part and read its drawing (Drawing opens it). Then make it from bar: choose a tool, start the spindle, and move the tool against the work. Measure the part against the drawing whenever you stop.

  • Move the tool by dragging it in the picture, one slide at a time as if you were turning one handwheel; with the handwheel buttons, which repeat while held; with the arrow keys once the picture is selected; or by typing a position and pressing Feed to Z or Feed to X. Stop feed, or Escape, stops a feed part-way.
  • The spindle has to be running for anything to cut, and stopped before you change a tool, change the drill size or thread pitch, or measure the part. A caliper or micrometer never goes on turning work.
  • Each tool does only its own kind of work. When a move would ask a tool for something it cannot do, the simulator stops the tool there and says why. What the tool in use can and cannot do is listed under the tool rack. Turn / face offers two actual tools in its Cutting tool selector; stop the spindle before changing between them.
  • Undo takes back one cut at a time. New bar starts the part again, and undo brings the old bar back.
  • Measure compares every feature with the drawing. The list under the simulator says what each feature still needs, or whether it has already gone too far to save.
Each tool does one kind of work, and the knurl does not cut at all

Each tool does one kind of work, and the knurl does not cut at all

Facing, turning, drilling, threading and knurling are not the same action with a different shape of tool. Each tool reaches different places and moves in different ways.

Turning tool
The roughing tool supplied here has a 10° lead and a 0.008 in nose radius. Its angled edge reaches ahead of its readout point. Stopping an axial pass leaves an angled shoulder; leave allowance instead of running the nose to the finished shoulder plane.
Facing tool
A square, 1/16 in wide finishing blade set for radial feed. Put its left corner at the finished Z and feed X across the end or shoulder. Its actual sweep removes the allowance and leaves the face flat. Retract clear before moving Z. These are the lab’s selected tools; other turning tools and settings can both turn and face.
Chamfer tool
A 90° point. Plunged at an edge, each side cuts a 45° chamfer.
Grooving and parting blade
Cuts only on its front edge. Plunged part of the way it makes a groove; plunged to the center, or into the hole, it parts the work off.
Center drill, drill, countersink
Fed from the tailstock along the axis. A center drill makes a small pilot and a 60° seat for a lathe center; a spotting drill has different starting geometry. The twist drill makes the hole and the countersink chamfers its mouth. Choose a real drill’s starting method and spot angle from its maker’s guidance.
Boring bar
Turns the inside of a hole that is already there, the way the turning tool works on the outside. Its bar has to fit in the hole.
Threading tools
Form tools with a 60° point, one for outside threads and one on a bar for inside threads. For a threading pass the carriage is driven by the leadscrew, so the tool moves one thread pitch for every turn of the work.
Knurling tool
A straddle head with two opposed forming wheels, with left-hand and right-hand diagonal teeth. Their axles lie parallel to Z; together they roll a diamond pattern. Gap Ø is a simulated gap/contact-diameter control. A real tool’s arm adjustment and locking are separate from cross-slide infeed. The picture shows the barrels and axles in side projection; the highlighted rims are the forming contact.

What makes the simulator stop a move. Each of these is something the real tool cannot do, or should not be asked to:

  • The spindle is stopped, so the tool would only rub.
  • More of the cutting edge would be in the work than the tool takes in one pass. Take it in more passes.
  • A part of the tool that does not cut would touch the work: the holder, the top of an insert, the bar of a boring tool, the side of a blade.
  • The tool would hit the chuck jaws.
  • A threading tool is still in the thread when the carriage moves. Back it out first.
  • A knurl is pressed past full depth, or into a shoulder.
  • A drill is three of its own diameters into a cut without being backed out to clear its chips.

The simulator’s limits are teaching values chosen for these four parts. A real tool’s limits come from its maker and depend on the machine, the material and the setup.

Tool shape and setting matter: Sherline’s tool-grinding guide describes cutting edges, clearance and form tools. The particular blade widths, nose radius and operating limits used here are declared teaching choices, not specifications for every lathe tool.

Most parts start with a facing cut and end with parting

Most parts start with a facing cut and end with parting

More than one order can make the same part, and the simulator accepts any order that gets there. Some orders are still better than others, for reasons you can see in the work.

  • Face first. The faced end is the datum: every length on the drawing is measured from it. A sawn end is neither flat nor square to the axis.
  • Rough, then finish. A large step comes off in several passes, and only the last one goes to the size on the drawing. On the stepped pin, stop the roughing passes 0.040 in short of each shoulder, retract clear and change to the facing tool. With its left corner at the final shoulder Z, feed X to the smaller diameter. A deeper shoulder needs more clearance for the angled edge; the facing blade can remove its allowance in slices up to 0.0625 in wide.
  • Drill, then bore to size. The boring bar needs a hole its bar fits in. A center drill is available here to explore its pilot and center-seat shape, but it is not a universal prerequisite for drilling. On a real machine, use the starting method recommended for the following drill.
  • Heavy work before thin sections. Knurling pushes hard on the work. Knurling before the thin sections next to it are turned keeps the work stiff while it happens.
  • Make room for the threading tool. A thread needs somewhere for the tool to stop: a relief groove, or a stop short of the shoulder. Chamfer the end first so the thread starts on a clean edge.
  • Chamfer the back edge before parting. Once the part is cut off, its back edge is out of reach without a second setup.
  • Part off last. The part falls free, and anything not done to it by then needs another setup.

The small Chuck end circle is a separate axial view, looking from the tailstock toward the chuck. Its forward-rotation arrow and animation run counterclockwise in that view. The main picture is longitudinal, not a view along the spindle. See the viewpoint diagram in Haas’s spindle-direction training, page 16.

A thread is cut in several passes along one helix

A thread is cut in several passes along one helix

For a threading pass the carriage is coupled to the leadscrew, so the tool advances exactly one pitch for every turn of the work: 1/16 in for 16 threads per inch. Every pass follows the same helix, so every pass deepens the same groove.

The section uses a schematic thread envelope. Its unhatched bands lie between the surviving crests and dashed roots; they are not solid annular thread teeth. A real single-start helix intersects opposite sides half a pitch apart. The model samples a thread profile for depth checks and preserves its material envelope for later cuts and parting. The carriage still stops at the requested Z, even between full turns. Sandvik explains the lead/pitch relation for single- and multi-start threads.

  • A little deeper each pass. The simulator allows 0.015 in of infeed per pass outside and 0.012 in inside. The thread is done when its roots reach the root diameter on the drawing.
  • Back out before you come back. At the end of a pass the tool is still in the groove. Bringing the carriage back without backing the tool out would cut the crests off.
  • Keep the pitch. A pass at another pitch cuts a second helix across the first: a crossed thread.
  • Leave somewhere to stop. The tool runs into a shoulder unless a relief groove gives it room, which is why the thumb screw has one.

Supporting detail: Addendum 7 — How a manual lathe keeps every pass on one helix.

A knurl moves metal instead of cutting it

A knurl moves metal instead of cutting it

The knurling tool makes no chips. Its wheels press a pattern into the turning work, and the metal they push aside has to go somewhere: it rises between their teeth. The diameter over the points ends up larger than the blank was.

Blank
The diameter turned before knurling. On these drawings it is not given: the knurled size is, and you work back to the blank.
Full points
The wheels pressed deep enough that the diamond points are fully formed. Too shallow leaves flat tops; pressing past full depth crushes and flakes the points.
Over the points
The knurled diameter, measured across the crests.

In the simulator the roots sink exactly as far as the crests rise, 0.010 in each at full depth, so a full knurl adds 0.020 in to the diameter. A real knurl’s growth depends on its pitch, the material and how hard it is pressed.

This paired-wheel forming arrangement supports feeding along Z after engagement. Dorian’s straddle setup instructions (H-19) and paired diagonal-wheel example (H-48) describe that combination. The drawing is a generic teaching head, not a dimensioned catalog tool or a setup instruction for a particular machine.

Things to try in the simulator

Things to try in the simulator

  • On the stepped pin, try to turn the body from 1.000 to 0.750 in in one pass. Read why the tool stops, then do it in two.
  • Stop a roughing pass short of a shoulder and Measure. Choose Face without cutting and measure again. Then make the radial facing cut: which geometry actually changed?
  • Face the end but stop the cut at X 0.200. Measure: what is left at the center?
  • Face 0.010 in past Z0 and make the rest of the pin to the readout. Measure the lengths. Which ones moved, and why?
  • On the bushing, bring the boring bar to the end before there is a hole. Then drill a 1/4 in hole and try again. Which drill gives the bar room?
  • Drill the bushing without the center drill and read the note under the inspection.
  • On the thumb screw, try a threading pass up to the head before cutting the relief groove.
  • Take one threading pass at 16 per inch, change to 13 and take another. Measure the thread.
  • Knurl the head straight on the 1.000 in bar, without turning a blank first. Measure it against the drawing.
  • On the knurled nut, part the ring off and watch where the blade breaks through.
What this simulator leaves out

What this simulator leaves out

The simulator is about which tool does what, in what order, to what size. It leaves out:

  • Speed and feed. The spindle is on or off. Spindle speed, feed rate and what they do to the cut are on Feeds and Speeds.
  • The cut itself. No tool wear, heat, chatter, deflection or surface finish. A drill cannot wander, so a hole started without a center drill is only noted, not drawn off center.
  • Setups. One setup only: no turning the part around, no second operation, no tailstock center supporting long work.
  • Threads and knurls, simplified. Thread pitch, crests and roots are checked along the required length; pitch diameter and functional thread fit are not verified. The form knurl illustrates displaced material and diameter growth. Its patterned section is schematic, not an exact volume-conservation calculation. Form and cut knurling use different mechanisms.
  • Its numbers. Inch only. The tolerances, the tool limits and the parts are teaching values, not tool-maker data and not a standard.

Tolerances on the drawings mean the same as on Tolerances and Fits: a size on a limit passes.

The starting method for a real hole depends on the drill. For example, Haas distinguishes center drilling from spotting for carbide twist drills; this model does not predict drill wandering.

Machining/Measurement and Fit

Surface Texture and Finish

A machined surface has a lay, a waviness and a roughness; a stylus trace and a filter turn them into Ra, Rz and Rt, and a drawing symbol says what is required and how the surface may be made.

A surface has lay, waviness and roughness

A surface has lay, waviness and roughness

Every manufactured surface carries marks from the process that made it. Surface texture describes those marks: which way they run, how far apart they are, and how tall they stand.

Roughness
The finest, closely spaced marks, such as the feed marks a cutting tool leaves at each pass or the scratches of abrasive grit.
Waviness
A longer, gentler undulation that the roughness sits on, for example from vibration or deflection while the part was made.
Lay
The direction of the main surface pattern, set by how the tool or the part moved.
Form
The overall shape, such as a face that is slightly curved. Size and geometric tolerances control form; surface texture is what is left on top of it.
A stylus traces one line, and a filter splits it

A stylus traces one line, and a filter splits it

A contact instrument drags a fine stylus along a straight line and records its height. That record is the measured profile. Everything else is worked out from it.

Trace direction
Usually across the lay, so the stylus crosses the marks. If the drawing specifies a measuring direction, that direction governs.
Mean line
A smooth line the filter draws through the measured profile, a weighted average of the heights around each point. This mean line is the waviness.
Cutoff λc
The wavelength where the filter splits the profile. Undulations much longer than λc stay in the mean line; marks much shorter than λc are left over for the roughness. A wave exactly λc long is shared half and half.
Roughness profile
The measured profile minus the mean line.
Evaluation length
The part of the trace the numbers come from. In this lab it is five sections, each λc long. The trace runs one more λc at each end so the filter has heights on both sides of every evaluated point.

The filter decides what counts as roughness, not the size of the undulation. Change λc and the same undulation can move from the waviness into the roughness. That is why a measurement result needs its cutoff, and why a drawing or its standard says which one applies.

Ra, Rz and Rt read the roughness differently

Ra, Rz and Rt read the roughness differently

All three come from the same roughness profile. They answer different questions about it. This lab uses the older ISO 4287 convention with five sections for Rz; the drawing-symbol comparison separately shows older and current graphics.

Ra
The average distance of the roughness profile from its mean line over the evaluation length. Peaks and valleys count alike.
Rz
The average of the sections’ peak-to-valley heights. Each section counts once, whatever is in it.
Rt
The largest peak-to-valley height over the whole evaluation length: the single highest peak to the single deepest valley.

Ra = average of |roughness| over the evaluation length

Rz = (Z1 + Z2 + Z3 + Z4 + Z5) ÷ 5

For the trace above: Ra 1.55 µm; Rz = (6.55 + 6.56 + 6.70 + 6.57 + 6.87) ÷ 5 = 6.65 µm; Rt 7.10 µm.

The values are in micrometres (µm). They can also be given in microinches (µin): one inch is exactly 25.4 mm, so 1 µin is exactly 0.0254 µm, and Ra 1.6 µm is 63.0 µin.

Name the standard. Current documents use the ISO 21920 series. Many existing drawings and instruments use the older ISO 4287 parameters and ISO 1302 symbols. The names Ra, Rz and Rt carried over, but the standards are not identical, so this page says which one each symbol comes from and does not mix them. For a real part, check which standard the drawing invokes.

Change the surface, the trace and the drawing, and watch the numbers. Start with experiment 1.

  • The plots are that trace: the measured profile with its mean line, then the roughness profile with its five sections.
  • The drawing holds one requirement against this one trace and writes it as a callout in the view you choose.

The same-Ra experiment is the figure in the next section.

Same Ra, different surfaces

Same Ra, different surfaces

These three roughness profiles all have Ra 1.6 µm. They are not the same surface. All three plots use the same height scale.

  • Ra alone cannot tell these apart.
  • Rz separates the rounded marks from the other two, but not flat tops from narrow peaks.
  • Where the extremes sit, above or below the mean line, separates those two.

One number does not describe a surface. That is why a drawing names the parameter, not just a value.

Reading a surface texture symbol

Reading a surface texture symbol

The symbol’s point touches the line that represents the surface in a drawing view. Its shape says how the surface may be made; the text beside it says what texture is required.

The three process requirements, in the older and the current graphics. Schematic drawings: the standards dimension the symbols exactly.
SymbolOlder, ISO 1302Current, ISO 21920-1Meaning
BasicAny manufacturing process is permitted. This does not forbid machining; it simply does not require it.
BarMaterial removal is required: the surface must be produced by removing material, for example by machining.
CircleMaterial removal is prohibited: the surface must not be machined or otherwise have material removed to meet this requirement.
Current or older
An ISO 21920-1 symbol carries a short separate dash above the short leg, touching neither leg. The older ISO 1302 graphic has none, so the familiar older marks are not the current symbols unchanged.
The requirement
The parameter and its limit, such as Ra 3.2, sit below the long line, to the right of the long leg, in both.
The lay
In an ISO 21920-1 callout the process and the lay sit above the long line. In the older symbols the lay symbol sits beside the long leg, below the line.

A complete specification can state more than this page draws, such as the measuring direction. The process mark is a requirement about how the surface is made; a profile measurement checks the texture, not whether material was removed.

Lay symbols belong to the drawing view

Lay symbols belong to the drawing view

A lay symbol says which way the marks run. = and ⊥ are judged against the plane of projection of the view the symbol is drawn in, not against the page or the screen.

The first two figures are the same surface. Its marks run front to back: parallel to the right side view’s plane of projection, so = there, and perpendicular to the front view’s, so ⊥ there. The arrow shows which way each view looks.

Lay and trace direction are different things. The lay says how the marks run. The trace direction says how they were measured; it is usually across the lay unless the drawing specifies one.

The lay symbols and meanings here are those of ISO 1302:2002.

Older notation: N grades and triangle marks

Older notation: N grades and triangle marks

Older drawings may give a roughness grade number or a row of triangles instead of a parameter and value.

Each grade number stands for one Ra value. A grade is an Ra value: it does not convert to Rz.

One requirement, four ways

Slide the Ra limit and compare the current symbol, the older symbol, the grade number and the triangle marks for the same value.

Read the callout

Read the callout

Ten short questions on the symbols, the lay, the older notations and what the numbers respond to.

  1. The older ISO 1302 symbol with a circle in its V, and Ra 3.2. May this surface be machined to reach Ra 3.2 µm? No: material removal is prohibited. The circle in the V prohibits material removal. Material removal is prohibited: the surface must not be machined or otherwise have material removed to meet this requirement.
  2. A current symbol with an open V, no connecting material-removal crossbar or circle, a separate identifying dash above the short leg, and Ra 6.3. Does this callout forbid machining the surface? No, any process is permitted. The V has no connecting material-removal crossbar or circle: it is the basic symbol. The separate floating dash identifies ISO 21920; it does not require machining. Any manufacturing process is permitted. This does not forbid machining; it simply does not require it.
  3. A symbol with a bar closing its V, a short separate dash above the short leg, and Ra 0.8. Which standard's graphic is this? ISO 21920-1 (current). The short separate dash above the short leg, touching neither leg, marks an ISO 21920-1 symbol. The older ISO 1302 graphic has no dash.
  4. A block of surface whose marks run front to back. An arrow shows the right side view looking at its right side. The marks run front to back. Which lay symbol belongs on this surface in the right side view? =. The right side view looks along the arrow. Marks running front to back are parallel to that view's plane of projection, so the symbol is =. The same surface takes ⊥ in the front view: the symbol depends on the view, not on the screen or page.
  5. A block of surface whose marks run front to back. An arrow shows the front view looking at its front. The marks run front to back. Which lay symbol belongs on this surface in the front view? ⊥. The front view looks along the arrow. Marks running front to back are perpendicular to that view's plane of projection, so the symbol is ⊥. The same surface takes = in the right side view: the symbol depends on the view, not on the screen or page.
  6. The grade number N8. An older drawing gives grade N8. What does that stand for? Ra 3.2 µm. N8 stands for Ra 3.2 µm (126 µin). Each step of the grade number doubles or halves the Ra value, near enough.
  7. Three downward triangles. In the catalog comparison, which Ra values sit beside three triangles? 0.4, 0.8, 1.6 µm. Three triangles sit beside Ra 0.4, 0.8, 1.6 µm. The catalog calls this comparison approximate, not rigorous. Read it as a rough historical guide, not as acceptance limits.
  8. A current symbol with Rz 6.3. Which N grade means the same as this Rz 6.3 µm requirement? None: grades are Ra values. Grade numbers each stand for an Ra value; N9 is Ra 6.3 µm, not Rz 6.3 µm. Ra and Rz measure different things, and how they compare depends on the shape of the profile, as the same-Ra experiment in the lab shows.
  9. One deep scratch crosses this otherwise even trace. Which number has the largest proportional change? Rt. In the lab, a scratch three times the mark height takes Rt from 7.10 to 23.4 µm, Rz from 6.65 to 10.5 µm and Ra from 1.55 to 1.88 µm. Rt spans the highest peak to the deepest valley over the whole length. Rz averages five section heights, diluting localized extremes; filtering can spread a scratch across section boundaries. Ra averages every point.
  10. A block of surface with parallel marks running front to back, and a stylus trace running left to right across them. The trace on this surface crosses the marks. Traced along the marks instead, Ra would be: Much smaller. In the lab, Ra is 1.55 µm across the marks and 0.328 µm along them: the stylus misses the marks when it runs beside them. Tracing across the lay is the usual choice, but a direction the drawing specifies governs.
What this lab leaves out

What this lab leaves out

The lab is a teaching model of one straight trace. A real measurement and a real acceptance decision involve more:

  • The instrument. A real stylus has a tip radius, and instruments apply a short-wavelength filter and remove the part’s form before filtering. The lab’s stylus is sharp and its part is flat.
  • The filter and parameters. This lab follows the older ISO 4287 teaching convention of five sections for Rz, with a Gaussian mean line having 50% transmission at λc. Dense samples resolve the narrow marks; numerical integration on a coarser grid computes the smooth mean line. This is not a compliant instrument or a complete ISO 21920 inspection setup, and a drawing or standard can call for other settings.
  • The decision. The lab compares one trace with one limit. The drawing and its standard say how many traces are taken, where, and how the results are judged.
  • The process. No trace shows whether material was removed. The process requirement is checked against how the part was made.
  • Scratches and pits. Whether an isolated flaw counts against a texture requirement is for the drawing and its standard to say.
  • Symbols. The drawings are schematic. The lay symbols are those of ISO 1302:2002; the lab writes the same symbols in the ISO 21920-1 lay position. Check the current standard before relying on one there. Inch-drawing (ASME) practice is not covered here.

Machining/Measurement and Fit

Tolerances and Fits

The permitted size ranges on a hole and a shaft decide whether the two have clearance, interference, or could have either.

A size tolerance gives two limits

A size tolerance gives two limits

Manufacturing produces variation. For each diameter in this lab, the drawing gives a size between two limits. A measured diameter inside that interval passes this size check.

Nominal size
The size a feature is named by, such as Ø0.7500 in. Ø means diameter. Every limit is measured from this number.
Deviation
How far a limit sits above (+) or below (−) nominal. +0.0010 puts a limit 0.0010 in above it.
Limits
Nominal plus each deviation: the largest and smallest sizes that pass inspection. Ø0.7500 +0.0010 / 0.0000 means anything from 0.7500 in to 0.7510 in.
Tolerance
The width of that range: largest limit minus smallest limit. Here, 0.0010 in.

A size exactly on a limit passes. On this page the limits are part of the allowed range: a 0.7500 in hole and a 0.7510 in hole are both good. A 0.7511 in hole is not.

Clearance is the hole size minus the shaft size

Clearance is the hole size minus the shaft size

Put a shaft in a hole and the number that decides the fit is the difference between their two diameters.

clearance = hole size − shaft size

  • Positive: the hole is bigger. There is a gap, and the shaft slides in.
  • Negative: the shaft is bigger. That is interference: on paper the parts overlap, so the shaft has to be pressed in, or it does not go at all.
  • Zero: exactly the same size, called line-to-line. No gap and no overlap.

Clearance is measured across the whole diameter. With the shaft centred in the hole, the gap you would see on each side is half of it:

gap on each side = clearance ÷ 2

Three kinds of fit, decided by the two worst cases

Three kinds of fit, decided by the two worst cases

You do not have to check every pair of parts a drawing allows. Two pairs settle it: the tightest and the loosest.

Tightest legal pair
The smallest hole with the largest shaft. Its clearance is the least any good pair can have:
hole minimum − shaft maximum
Loosest legal pair
The largest hole with the smallest shaft. Its clearance is the most any good pair can have:
hole maximum − shaft minimum
The fit is named by where those two numbers land.
FitTightest pairLoosest pairWhat it means
Clearancegap, or exactly zerogapNo permitted pair has dimensional overlap. Equality has no gap.
TransitionoverlapgapSome good pairs slide together; some have to be pressed.
Interferenceoverlapoverlap, or exactly zeroNo permitted pair has a positive gap. Equality has no overlap.

The zero cases are deliberate. When the tightest pair comes out at exactly zero, every good pair either has a gap or just meets, so this page counts it as a clearance fit and the lab marks it zero at the limit. The same goes the other way for interference.

Fit lab: make two parts, then try them together

Fit lab: make two parts, then try them together

Pick a drawing, then set the size each part actually came out at. Watch whether each part passes inspection, and whether the two go together.

  • The section view is the pair you made, cut in half. The gold and blue bands are where each wall is allowed to be.
  • The pair map is every pair the drawing allows. Anything above the diagonal has a shaft bigger than its hole.
The lab’s example drawings. All are made-up teaching limits on a Ø0.7500 in nominal, not values from any standard.
DrawingHole limitsShaft limitsTightest pairLoosest pairFit
Slides freely0.7500 to 0.75100.7480 to 0.7490+0.0010+0.0030Clearance
